archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (pass-defense problem)
archetype.definition: A roughly average offense paired with a pass defense that leaks underneath. The Jets have played like a below-average team, not a 2-7 one, and lost most of the coin-flip games along the way.

report.headline: Better than 2-7, but a leaky pass defense keeps losing close games.
report.take:
The 2026 Jets are a real step up from the team that bottomed out last year. In 2025 they finished last in the league in net EPA at -0.271. This year they sit 23rd at -0.055. The offense has climbed from 29th to 17th in EPA per play, with Geno Smith starting every game and the passing attack grading 15th. That is not a good team. It is a mediocre one, and mediocre teams usually don't start 2-7.

The gap between play and record comes from two places. The first is close games. They are 28th in one-score win rate at 0.167, and the point differential of -41 implies 3.7 wins, not 2. That is the -1.7 wins over expected. Green Bay by three, Miami by three, Las Vegas by five and Detroit and New England by seven were all winnable. The second is a pass defense that cannot hold up. It is 30th in pass EPA allowed and 30th in success rate allowed, and the real hole is the short game: 31st in EPA allowed on short throws. Offenses don't need to beat the Jets deep. They complete the easy ones and move the chains, and the defense is 23rd on third downs and 22nd in red-zone touchdown rate.

The numbers flatter the run defense a little. The per-play rush EPA allowed ranks 10th and the tackling is genuinely sound at 5th in missed-tackle rate. But Chicago ran for 232 and Kansas City for 163, so opponents can still grind on them when the game script lets them. On offense, the protection is the weak link. They have taken 28 sacks, 29th in the league, and convert only 0.471 of short-yardage tries (31st), which undercuts an aggressive fourth-down approach.

The path from here is a split season in miniature. The offense found a rhythm in October, putting up 25 on Miami and 33 on Las Vegas. The defense went the other way, allowing 26, 28, 38 and 35 over the last four games, and every game since the Week 5 win over Cleveland has been a loss. Now Garrett Wilson, the target leader by a wide margin, is out with a concussion for Buffalo. Several secondary and linebacker bodies are out too. The schedule softens soon after, with the 0-8 Chargers and the 1-7 Dolphins, and that is where some of the close-game bad luck should start to pay back.

strengths.title: A functional, efficient passing offense
strengths.body: The passing game grades 15th in EPA, and the offense is 11th in success rate, a huge leap from last year's 29th-ranked unit. Smith has started every week, which gives the offense continuity it hasn't had. When protected, they can move the ball: 287 passing yards against Miami and 290 against Las Vegas. Wilson's absence tests how deep that efficiency really goes.

strengths.title: Sure tackling and a stout run front
strengths.body: The Jets rank 5th in missed-tackle rate and 10th in rush EPA allowed, so ball carriers rarely break loose on a per-play basis. That is a stable, skill-driven trait and should travel. The caveat is volume: when opponents get ahead and lean on the run, the yards still pile up.

strengths.title: Protecting the football
strengths.body: Only 7 giveaways in nine games against 10 takeaways puts the turnover margin at +3. That is a rare positive for a 2-7 team and a sharp reversal from last season's league-worst margin. Takeaways are fickle, but low giveaway totals tend to hold with a steady veteran quarterback.

concerns.title: Underneath pass defense gets carved
concerns.body: The Jets are 31st in EPA allowed on short passes, 30th in pass EPA allowed and 30th in success rate allowed. That is a structural flaw, not a few big plays. They give up efficient completions that extend drives, which is why third downs and red-zone defense also rank in the bottom third. With a cornerback, a safety and a linebacker on the injury report, it is unlikely to fix itself quickly.

concerns.title: Sacks and short-yardage failures
concerns.body: The line has allowed 28 sacks, 26th in sack rate, including five each against Detroit and Kansas City. The overall pressure rate (19th) is less alarming than the sacks, which points partly to Smith holding the ball. The run game also fails when it matters most, 31st in short-yardage conversion. Both stall drives that the passing efficiency otherwise sustains.

concerns.title: Losing the coin flips
concerns.body: A 0.167 one-score win rate and -1.7 wins over expected say much of 2-7 is variance. Self-inflicted damage plays a part: they are 25th in penalties per game, and 156 penalty yards sank a three-point loss to Green Bay. The luck part should regress, but the penalty part is on them.

trend.note: The offense peaked in October with 25 and 33 points against Miami and Las Vegas, but the defense has given up 26 or more in each of the last four games. Every game since the Week 5 win has been a loss, capped by a 12-35 rout at Kansas City.

nextGame.headline: Without Garrett Wilson, the Jets need a ground game and turnovers.
nextGame.body:
Buffalo arrives at 7-1 with the league's best offense by EPA and points per game, but a defense that ranks 29th in EPA allowed. That sets up a game where the Jets' biggest problem, short pass defense, meets a passing attack ranked 3rd in EPA. The Bills' weaknesses, a 30th-ranked missed-tackle rate and middling rush defense, are areas the Jets can test. The Book has Buffalo by 8.5 with a 50.5 total, and the Jets are +410 on the moneyline. The Bills have been fortunate too, with 1.7 wins over expected and a 0.8 one-score win rate.

Availability cuts both ways. The Jets lose Garrett Wilson (concussion, 89% snaps, the team's top target). That pushes Adonai Mitchell and the tight ends, Kenyon Sadiq and Mason Taylor, up the pecking order. Joseph Ossai (45% snaps) is also out on the edge, along with a thinned secondary and linebacker group. Buffalo is missing left tackle Dion Dawkins (99% snaps) and tackle Alec Anderson, which weakens an offensive line that has been among the league's best in pass protection and run blocking.

waysToWin.title: Run it and shrink the game
waysToWin.body: Buffalo's run defense is 18th in rush EPA allowed and the Bills miss tackles at the 30th-ranked rate. The Jets' backs average 4.11 yards a carry. Long, run-heavy drives keep Josh Allen's offense on the sideline and turn a shootout into a game the Jets can stay inside of.

waysToWin.title: Pressure a patched-up tackle group
waysToWin.body: With Dawkins and Anderson out, Buffalo's protection is weaker than its 5th-ranked sacks-allowed figure suggests. The Jets rank 10th in sack rate and showed their ceiling with eight sacks against Cleveland. Collapsing the pocket is the only reliable way to slow this passing game.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle
waysToWin.body: Buffalo is 22nd in turnover differential per game, while the Jets protect the ball. A short field or two is the most plausible way an 8.5-point underdog steals a division game.

waysToLose.title: Buffalo dinks its way downfield
waysToLose.body: The Bills' passing attack ranks 3rd in EPA, and the Jets are 31st against short throws. Buffalo doesn't have to take risks. It can stack completions, convert third downs and score in the red zone the way Kansas City and Las Vegas did.

waysToLose.title: Pressure swamps a Wilson-less offense
waysToLose.body: Buffalo generates pressure at the league's 2nd-highest rate, and the Jets' line is 26th in sack rate. Without Wilson as the reliable outlet, holding the ball longer means more drive-killing sacks, like the five taken at Kansas City.

waysToLose.title: Bills' ground game wears them down
waysToLose.body: Even with the Jets' per-play run defense rated well, Buffalo is 1st in run success rate and 2nd in yards before contact. The Jets have given up big rushing totals lately. If Buffalo gets ahead and runs the clock, the Jets' best path of shortening the game disappears.

nextGame.watch: Who becomes the Jets' WR1 by targets without Wilson. Buffalo lets opposing WR1s score 5.3 PPR points over their average, 30th in the league. Whether Adonai Mitchell can claim that role decides whether the passing game stays efficient.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is roughly a 23rd-ranked unit by net EPA. It has an average offense and a bad pass defense, and its close-game luck should even out. The schedule after Buffalo has soft spots: the winless Chargers with the league's worst offense, a Miami team that ranks 32nd on defense, and an Arizona defense that ranks 29th. Those are the games where the Jets should be favored or close to it. Denver, New England, Minnesota's top-ranked defense and a trip to Buffalo are much harder.

Expect the offense to hold around its current level once Wilson returns, and the turnover margin to drift toward neutral. The pass defense is the part least likely to improve, given its depth of failure and the injuries. A handful of wins over the final stretch is realistic. A playoff push is not.
swingFactors: How quickly Garrett Wilson returns from the concussion
Whether the short pass defense stabilizes with the injured defensive backs back
Close-game results against LAC, MIA and ARI

confidence.note: Nine games of stable QB play, but injuries to the top receiver and secondary cloud the outlook.
